# Azure Platform — Activity Log and Resource Log Emission

Azure emits on two distinct planes, and both are required for AU-2 coverage of
the Azure estate.

**Control plane — the activity log.** Every create, update, delete, and action
executed through Azure Resource Manager, plus policy evaluations, Defender for
Cloud alerts, and service/resource health. One diagnostic setting per
subscription. This is *who changed what* in the estate.

**Resource plane — resource logs.** What happens *inside* a resource: Key Vault
secret reads, storage-account data operations, SQL audit events, firewall
flows. One diagnostic setting per resource, per resource type, with
type-specific categories.

An agency that has configured only the activity log can prove a Key Vault was
created and cannot prove which secrets were read out of it.

## Part 1 — Activity log

### Categories

| Category | Contains |
|---|---|
| `Administrative` | Every create / update / delete / action through Resource Manager, **including all Azure RBAC changes in the subscription** |
| `Security` | Alerts generated by Microsoft Defender for Cloud |
| `Policy` | All effect-action operations by Azure Policy — `Audit`, `Deny` |
| `ServiceHealth` | Azure service-health incidents affecting your resources |
| `ResourceHealth` | Resource health-status transitions — Available, Unavailable, Degraded, Unknown |
| `Alert` | Azure Monitor alert activations |
| `Autoscale` | Autoscale engine operations |
| `Recommendation` | Azure Advisor recommendations |

Definitions from the
[Azure Activity Log event schema](https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/azure-monitor/platform/activity-log-schema#categories);
the enumerable list is confirmed by
[`Get-AzEventCategory`](https://learn.microsoft.com/powershell/module/az.monitor/get-azeventcategory?view=azps-16.2.0).

`Administrative`, `Security`, and `Policy` are the AU-2 / AU-12 core.
`Administrative` in particular carries RBAC changes, which is the AC-2 and
AC-6 evidence stream for the Azure estate — there is no separate RBAC audit
log to fall back on.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Enable all eight

The activity log is low-volume relative to resource logs and there is no
meaningful cost argument for selective enablement. `ServiceHealth` and
`ResourceHealth` in particular become valuable during incident
reconstruction, when you need to rule out a platform cause before attributing
an outage to an attack.
:::

### Portal

1. In the [Azure portal](https://portal.azure.com), open **Monitor** →
   **Activity log**.
2. Select **Export Activity Logs**.
3. Select the subscription, then **Add diagnostic setting**.
4. Name the setting, check all applicable categories, choose the destination.
5. **Save**.

Export typically begins within about **30 minutes**
([configuring activity log export](https://learn.microsoft.com/troubleshoot/azure/azure-monitor/activity-logs/config-export/configuring-azure-activity-log-export-comprehensive-guide)).

### CLI

The activity log needs the **subscription** subcommand — the plain
`az monitor diagnostic-settings create` is resource-scoped and will not do it:

```bash
az monitor diagnostic-settings subscription create \
  --name "uiao-activity-log-export" \
  --location "usgovvirginia" \
  --workspace "/subscriptions/${SUBSCRIPTION_ID}/resourceGroups/${RG}/providers/Microsoft.OperationalInsights/workspaces/${WORKSPACE}" \
  --logs '[
    {"category": "Administrative",  "enabled": true},
    {"category": "Security",        "enabled": true},
    {"category": "Policy",          "enabled": true},
    {"category": "ServiceHealth",   "enabled": true},
    {"category": "ResourceHealth",  "enabled": true},
    {"category": "Alert",           "enabled": true},
    {"category": "Autoscale",       "enabled": true},
    {"category": "Recommendation",  "enabled": true}
  ]'
```

::: {.callout-warning}
## `New-AzDiagnosticSetting` cannot export the activity log

Microsoft states it plainly: "You can't use this method for an activity log.
Instead, create an Azure Resource Manager template and deploy it by using
PowerShell"
([diagnostic settings in Azure Monitor](https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/azure-monitor/platform/diagnostic-settings#methods-for-creating-a-diagnostic-setting)).

PowerShell-first shops routinely write a `New-AzDiagnosticSetting` call for
the activity log, see it fail or silently no-op, and conclude the activity log
"doesn't support export." Use `az monitor diagnostic-settings subscription
create`, or a subscription-scope ARM/Bicep deployment.
:::

### Bicep at subscription scope

```bicep
// activity-log-export.bicep
// az deployment sub create --location <region> --template-file activity-log-export.bicep
targetScope = 'subscription'

param workspaceId string
param settingName string = 'uiao-activity-log-export'

var categories = [
  'Administrative'
  'Security'
  'Policy'
  'ServiceHealth'
  'ResourceHealth'
  'Alert'
  'Autoscale'
  'Recommendation'
]

resource activityLogExport 'Microsoft.Insights/diagnosticSettings@2021-05-01-preview' = {
  name: settingName
  properties: {
    workspaceId: workspaceId
    logs: [for category in categories: {
      category: category
      enabled: true
    }]
  }
}
```

Landing zones with a management-group hierarchy can set this once at the top
level instead of per subscription: a management-group diagnostic setting
"exports Azure Monitor activity log events for that management group in
addition to all management groups under it in the hierarchy"
([activity log](https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/azure-monitor/platform/activity-log#export-management-group-activity-logs)).

::: {.callout-note}
## Duplicates are the intended trade-off

If both a management group and a subscription beneath it carry diagnostic
settings, you receive duplicate events. Microsoft's position is that
"getting duplicate events is better than missing events," because the
`hierarchy` property is not populated by resource providers outside Resource
Manager, so their events do not propagate upward.

Deduplicate at query time rather than by removing a setting:

```kusto
AzureActivity
| extend Hash = hash(dynamic_to_json(pack_all()))
| summarize arg_max(TimeGenerated, *) by Hash
```

For a federal tenant this is the right call — an assessor accepts a
deduplicated stream; nobody accepts a gap.
:::

## Part 2 — Resource logs

Resource logs are per-resource and the category list varies by resource type.
Discover what a given resource supports before writing the setting:

```bash
az monitor diagnostic-settings categories list \
  --resource "${RESOURCE_ID}" \
  --query "value[].{name:name, type:categoryType, group:categoryGroups}" -o table
```

Then create the setting. `allLogs` is a category *group* meaning "every log
category this resource type has," which is the correct default for a
compliance baseline — it survives Microsoft adding a category later:

```bash
az monitor diagnostic-settings create \
  --name "uiao-resource-logs" \
  --resource "${RESOURCE_ID}" \
  --workspace "${WORKSPACE_RESOURCE_ID}" \
  --logs '[{"categoryGroup": "allLogs", "enabled": true}]' \
  --metrics '[{"category": "AllMetrics", "enabled": true}]' \
  --export-to-resource-specific true
```

::: {.callout-tip}
## Use resource-specific tables

`--export-to-resource-specific true` (ARM: `logAnalyticsDestinationType:
'Dedicated'`) sends logs to purpose-built tables instead of the generic
`AzureDiagnostics` table. Microsoft recommends this
([Azure Monitor REST API guidance](https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/managed-instance-apache-cassandra/monitor-clusters#diagnostic-settings-in-azure)).

It matters for compliance work specifically: `AzureDiagnostics` is a shared,
sparsely-populated wide table with a **column limit** that different resource
types compete for. Once that limit is hit, new columns are silently dropped —
audit fields disappear from records that otherwise look intact. Resource-
specific tables have their own schema and cannot be crowded out.

The trade-off is that detection rules must name the specific table. Decide
once, apply everywhere; mixing modes across a fleet is the worst outcome.
:::

::: {.callout-warning}
## The self-reference loop

A storage account or Event Hubs namespace cannot be the destination for its
own diagnostic setting — it would generate data by writing data, forever. The
portal blocks this; the CLI, PowerShell, REST API, and ARM templates **do
not**
([diagnostic settings](https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/azure-monitor/platform/diagnostic-settings#methods-for-creating-a-diagnostic-setting)).

Automation that enumerates every resource in a subscription and applies a
diagnostic setting will eventually hit the logging storage account itself.
Exclude the telemetry-infrastructure resources explicitly in any at-scale
loop.
:::

## Part 3 — Enforce at scale with Azure Policy

Everything above configures what exists today. A resource created tomorrow is
born silent unless policy makes emission a property of the platform rather
than a deployment checklist item.

Use built-in `DeployIfNotExists` policy initiatives, assigned at management-
group scope with a managed identity holding **Monitoring Contributor** on the
target scope and **Log Analytics Contributor** on the workspace:

| Policy pattern | Effect |
|---|---|
| *Deploy Diagnostic Settings for `<resource type>` to Log Analytics workspace* | `DeployIfNotExists` — remediates new and, via a remediation task, existing resources |
| *Configure Azure Activity logs to stream to specified Log Analytics workspace* | `DeployIfNotExists` at subscription scope |
| *Audit diagnostic setting* | `AuditIfNotExists` — reports without changing, for the assessment-only posture |

::: {.callout-important}
## `DeployIfNotExists` only fires on resource writes

A `DeployIfNotExists` assignment evaluates when a resource is created or
updated. It does **not** retroactively fix the estate at assignment time —
existing resources stay non-compliant until you run a **remediation task**
against the assignment.

The standard failure: policy is assigned, the compliance dashboard goes green
for newly-created resources, and a year of pre-existing resources continues
emitting nothing. Assign the policy *and* run the remediation task, then
confirm the compliance percentage against the resource count.
:::

This is also the direct implementation of FedRAMP **KSI-MLA-EVC** — "the
configuration of machine-based information resources, especially
infrastructure as code, is persistently evaluated and tested." A policy
assignment with continuous compliance evaluation *is* the persistent
evaluation; a spreadsheet of resources somebody checked once is not.

The repo's Azure Arc policy library covers the adjacent hybrid-server case:
[Azure Arc policy library](../../substrate/platform-tooling/azure-arc-policy-library.qmd).

## Verify emission

```kusto
// Azure control-plane emission health, by subscription and category.
AzureActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(24h)
| summarize Events = count(), LastEvent = max(TimeGenerated)
    by SubscriptionId, Category
| extend Stale = LastEvent < ago(6h)
| order by Stale desc, SubscriptionId asc, Category asc
```

A subscription absent from these results is not exporting. Compare the
returned `SubscriptionId` set against the full subscription inventory —
the query cannot show you a subscription that has never sent a single event,
which is exactly the one you need to find:

```bash
# Subscriptions with no activity-log diagnostic setting.
for sub in $(az account list --query "[].id" -o tsv); do
  count=$(az monitor diagnostic-settings subscription list \
            --subscription "$sub" --query "length(value)" -o tsv 2>/dev/null || echo 0)
  [ "$count" -eq 0 ] && echo "NO ACTIVITY LOG EXPORT: $sub"
done
```

Resource-level coverage, for resources that have emitted at least once:

```kusto
// Resource types currently landing in the generic diagnostics table.
AzureDiagnostics
| where TimeGenerated > ago(24h)
| summarize Events = count(), LastEvent = max(TimeGenerated) by ResourceType, ResourceProvider
| order by Events desc
```

Neither query proves *completeness* — only Azure Policy compliance state
does, because it evaluates against the full resource inventory rather than
against what happens to have arrived. Treat the policy compliance percentage
as the AU-2 coverage metric and these queries as liveness checks on top of it.
